title: How to answer a system design question
dek: The same six steps for every question, how long to spend on each, and what the interviewer is listening for at each one. Every question in this section follows them.

items: Pin down what to build before drawing anything: three or so features, what's out of scope, and a few qualities with numbers.
Name the main things the system stores, then write the API calls the features need.
Draw a simple design that handles every feature end to end. Caches, queues and shards come after it works.
Use the remaining time to make it hold up: the numbers, the failure cases, and the part the interviewer pushes on.
Talk while you work, do maths only when it changes a decision, and leave room for the interviewer to steer.

body.cap: A 45-minute interview, roughly: requirements 5 minutes, entities 2, API 5, a high-level design 15, deep dives 13, and the last 5 for your questions. Spending 20 minutes on requirements or skipping straight to sharding are the two most common ways to run out of time.

body.x: Building a house for a client. You ask how many people will live there and what they need, sketch the rooms, check the plumbing reaches every one, and only then argue about the brand of tiles.

Ask questions like a product manager would. Settle on about three features the system must do and say a few things it won't do in this interview. Then name three to five qualities, each with a number where you can: how fast, how many, how available, how consistent.

items: Features as user actions: "a restaurant creates a short link", "a customer opens it". Not technology.
Out of scope, said out loud: "I'll leave out user accounts and custom domains". It shows judgement and saves time.
Qualities with numbers: "redirects in under 100 ms", "links never point to the wrong page", "99.9% of redirects work".
Note what's unusual about the system. A URL shortener is read a hundred times more than it's written; a payment system must never charge twice. That one fact drives most of the design.

body.x: Don't fill a page with estimates up front. Do a calculation when its answer changes a choice: whether one database can take the writes, whether the hot data fits in memory, whether you need to shard. Say why you're doing it: "let me check whether one machine can hold this".
Keep the handful of conversions in your head: a day is about 10⁵ seconds, 10 lakh requests a day is about 12 a second, peaks are 2–3 times the average. The Quick Notes page has the rest.

items: List the nouns the system stores, as a rough first pass: link, click, user. Fields can wait until the design needs them.
Write one API call per feature. REST is the default: `POST /links`, `GET /{code}`. Use another style only when you can say why.
Take the user from their login token, not from the request body, so nobody can act as someone else.
For pipelines with many steps (upload, process, publish), list the steps in order before drawing; it keeps the design honest.

body.x: Draw the simplest set of boxes that serves every API call, then walk through each call in turn: where the request enters, what it reads and writes, what it returns. Write the key fields next to each data store as you go. If you see where a cache or a queue will be needed, say so and leave it for the deep dives.
The goal at the end of this step is a design that works. A complete, simple design beats a half-finished clever one.

Now make the design meet its numbers and survive failures. Pick the two or three hardest parts, often the ones the qualities point to, and improve each. A useful way to talk through each one is three steps:

body.name: First try
body.what: What most people would do first, and where it breaks.
body.use: Showing you see the problem, not just the fix.
body.ex: "Hash the URL and take the first 7 characters", then: "but two URLs can share a prefix".
body.like: The first draft of an essay.

body.name: Better
body.what: A change that removes the first try's flaw, with its own cost.
body.use: Most interviews: this is often enough at mid level.
body.ex: "Use a counter so codes never clash", then: "but one counter is a bottleneck".

body.name: Best
body.what: The choice that meets the numbers, and why its trade-offs are acceptable here.
body.use: Senior answers: say what you'd build and what you'd watch.
body.avoid: Over-building past what the requirements need.
body.ex: "Each server takes blocks of 1,000 IDs from the counter".

body.label: Roughly what interviewers look for
head: Level
Leads
Expected
rows: A clear end-to-end design; deep dives can follow the interviewer's prompts
Spots the hard parts unprompted, compares options with numbers, explains trade-offs
Picks the few decisions that matter most, covers failure and operations, keeps it simple

items: Designing before asking: building a global system when the interviewer wanted one city.
Naming technologies instead of reasons: "Kafka" is not an answer; "a log several services can read at their own pace" is.
Adding every component you know. Each box needs a requirement that asks for it.
Going quiet. The interviewer can only grade what they hear.
Never saying what could go wrong. Every design has a weak point; name it before you're asked.
Take a question from this section, set a 45-minute timer, and say your answer out loud or on paper before reading ours.
Compare: which requirements did you miss, which deep dive did you skip?
Build the design in the Lab and push traffic through it: you'll see which box gives out first.

body.x: Before your first question, try a Lab challenge: it's the high-level-design and deep-dive steps with numbers attached.
